claims.text: Isaiah Kenen's lobbying secured $65 million and $73 million in US aid for Israel in 1951–1952; in 1953 he formed the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs to separate lobbying from the American Zionist Council, partly over concerns about foreign-agent registration; it began operations in 1954 and was renamed the American Israel Public Affairs Committee in 1959.
Kenen retired in 1974 and was succeeded by Morris Amitay; Thomas Dine became executive director in 1980 and built AIPAC's grassroots campaign.
In 1982 and 1984 AIPAC-affiliated activists backed Richard Durbin against Rep. Paul Findley and Paul Simon against Sen. Charles Percy; both incumbents lost.

In 1992 AIPAC president David Steiner was secretly recorded by New York developer Haim Katz, who gave the tape to the Washington Times; Steiner claimed AIPAC had 'a dozen people in the campaign, in the headquarters, in Little Rock' and said 'we're just negotiating' over posts such as secretary of state; he called his statements untrue, apologized and resigned in November 1992.

Pentagon analyst Larry Franklin pleaded guilty in 2005 to passing classified information, including to two AIPAC officials; AIPAC fired Steven Rosen and Keith Weissman in April 2005; they were indicted under the Espionage Act, and all charges were dropped in 2009, the government citing rulings that made conviction unlikely and its unwillingness to expose classified information at trial.

Senator J. William Fulbright in the 1970s and former CIA official Victor Marchetti in the 1980s argued AIPAC should register under FARA; AIPAC says it is a registered lobbying group funded by private donations and receives no financial assistance from Israel or any other foreign group.

claims.text: AIPAC is a 501(c)(4) social-welfare organization in Washington, DC; donations to it are not tax-deductible. Its Forms 990 report revenue of $105.9M (FY2016), $133.9M (FY2019), $96.6M (FY2020), $73.5M (FY2022), $79.4M (FY2023), $156.4M (FY2024) and $122.5M (FY2025), with net assets of $177.6M at FY2025.
Howard Kohr was AIPAC's top-paid officer in most years shown, with reported compensation of $1,488,666 in FY2025.

The American Israel Education Foundation is a 501(c)(3) (exempt since July 1989); its Forms 990 report revenue of $59.2M (FY2024) and $61.1M (FY2025), expenses of $52.4M (FY2025) and net assets of $220.3M at FY2025.
AIPAC had 376 employees and 47 volunteers in 2022 and in 2025 reported more than 5 million members and 17 regional offices.
About 18,000 people attended AIPAC's March 2019 Policy Conference, including 4,000 students; nearly 20,000 delegates attended in 2016.
AIPAC held its last in-person Policy Conference in 2020; it cancelled the 2021 conference (held virtually) and the 2022 conference, citing pandemic uncertainty.

AIPAC reported lobbying spending of $3.5M in 2018 (OpenSecrets via Tablet), $3.3M in 2024 and almost $3.8M in 2025; J Street $595,000 (2024) and $750,000 (2025); ADL $1.4M and $1.5M; JFNA $455,350 and at least $689,360; RJC $200,000 and $300,000 (nine months); ZOA $180,000 and $200,000; Orthodox Union $350,000 in 2025.
AIPAC reported over $800,000 in lobbying in the fourth quarter of 2023; its PAC's fundraising averaged nearly $750,000 a week after 7 October 2023, more than twice the earlier average.
The Howard Center's travel database lists 868 AIEF-sponsored trips for 463 congressional offices from 2012 to 2023.
AIEF shares AIPAC's offices, board members and part of its logo (The Intercept).
In 2018 (OpenSecrets via Tablet) the National Association of Realtors reported $72.8M in lobbying, Boeing $15.1M, Amazon $14.4M and Exxon Mobil $11.2M.
Israel's prime minister addressed AIPAC's 2019 Policy Conference by satellite.
AIPAC's fiscal year ends in September (Forms 990).

claims.text: AIPAC announced in December 2021 that it would form a PAC and a super PAC ahead of the 2022 cycle; AIPAC PAC was created on 15 December 2021 and the United Democracy Project was formed on 3 January 2022.

In the 2022 cycle UDP raised almost $27.6M by 30 June and spent nearly $24.3M on independent expenditures by 2 August, all in Democratic contests; its top donors were AIPAC ($8.5M), Jan Koum ($2M), and Jonathon Jacobson, Paul Singer, Bernard Marcus and Haim Saban ($1M each). FactCheck.org found UDP the highest outside spender in the 2022 Democratic primaries; UDP's website said it works to help elect candidates who support the US–Israel relationship.

UDP's spokesman Patrick Dorton said it aimed 'to build the broadest bipartisan pro-Israel coalition in Congress possible' and cited 'rising concern in the pro-Israel community about candidates for Congress who held radical anti-Israel views'.

AIPAC PAC's 2022 endorsements included members who had voted against certifying the 2020 presidential election: by one account 37 of 130 endorsements announced in March 2022 (Wikipedia), and by J Street's count in August 2022, 109; asked whether any pro-Israel candidate could be ruled out, CEO Howard Kohr said 'I'd have to think about that'; J Street called for 'moral red lines'.

AIPAC's own memo of 7 November 2024 says its PAC endorsed 361 candidates in the 2024 cycle, that 326 won general elections (120 Democrats, 206 Republicans), that more than 10,000 members contributed over $53M to candidates, and that UDP helped decide nine races including the defeats of Bowman and Bush. It describes the PAC's giving as more than any other PAC's and AIPAC's aim as to 'encourage and persuade the U.S. government to enact specific policies'.

Per FEC filings and OpenSecrets, AIPAC and UDP spent $95.1M combined in 2024, up from $44M in 2022; RJC and its super PAC $19.7M (up from $4.5M); J Street $14.6M (from $8.6M); DMFI $4.8M (from $7.7M); NORPAC $2.7M (from $1.6M).

UDP raised about $104M in the 2026 cycle through June (more than the $87.1M raised in 2024), had spent about $52.5M, and per Politico routed more than 40 percent of its primary spending through pop-up and pass-through PACs; it spent around $61.4M in the 2024 cycle.

AIPAC's 2024 memo says its endorsements covered 75 percent of House members and 84 percent of senators in the cycle, and frames its legislative work around a $14.3 billion emergency package and an $18.1 billion funding package.
